script: Tricking My Slacker Coworker into Sabotaging Himself. I work in an office with a guy I'll call "Seth." He's the classic slacker, always scrolling his phone, popping into the bathroom every ten minutes, and if you ask him why he's late, he blames traffic like it's a national crisis. I tried to tell our boss about him a couple of times, but the audacity is that he always slipped out of trouble with a lame excuse. He'd always say, "I got a client call, I'll be right back," and then disappear for two hours. But here's the thing… Seth's favorite pastime is turning my life into a never-ending project. He'll ping me with "Can you help out with this?" and the real message is, "Do all the work while I take the credit." I've already lost a ton of sleep over that, and I've seen him get away with it so many times that I started to think my boss was blind. What I didn't know was that the last time he tried to dump a major report on me was about to become the ultimate plot twist. And that's when everything changed… The deadline for the client's report was in two days, and he slid the entire stack of spreadsheets onto my desk like a toddler dropping a plate. He was supposed to finish it himself, but I know the truth—he's just using me as a human calculator. If this didn't work, I'd lose everything: my reputation, my job, and maybe a future promotion. The stakes were higher than a $5 coffee. But here's the thing… I casually asked him if he was good with Excel, and he confessed he barely knew how to click a cell. That was my golden opportunity, bestie. I told him, "Sure, let me help you organize this." He didn't suspect a thing. What I didn't know was that I could slip in some hidden formulas that would mess up the data if he tried to copy it. I spent a few hours sprinkling dummy cells that would scramble numbers when he pasted them. The plan was simple: make him think everything was fine, then watch him choke on the invisible mess. And that's when everything changed… When he finally tried to copy the data into his report, the numbers flipped like a bad magic trick. Every time he hit "paste," a different column turned into gibberish. He stared at the screen, blinking like a kid seeing a magician's hat. The whole thing was a subtle sabotage, not a blatant sabotage. My heart was racing, but I kept my face cool. But here's the thing… The client called on the day it was due, furious because the report was filled with nonsense numbers. Seth was in a panic, his voice shaking as he tried to fix one part, only for another part to break. He came to me, hands trembling, begging for help.
